messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Mehta was 34 when a deliberate explosion tore through the downtown transit concourse he had been walking through on his lunch break. He worked as an urban planner for the city, and that day he had gone to the station to observe pedestrian flow around a redevelopment site. What remained with him was not a story he could tell from beginning to end, but a series of sharp pictures: a flash against the glass storefront, a man falling beside a newsstand, a child’s red backpack on the floor without the child in sight, gray dust hanging in the air as alarms screamed. Even in the first weeks afterward, when colleagues asked what happened, Arjun would stop and lose the thread. He could not place what came first and what came after; the images arrived without order, and the more he tried to force them into a coherent account, the more jumbled and unmanageable they felt.

In the months after the bombing, Arjun had come to believe that something essential in him had been damaged. Before, he had taken pride in being steady, analytic, and effective under pressure, the kind of planner who could walk a crowded block and instantly see patterns, conflicts, and solutions. Now he found himself thinking, with shame, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. He also became convinced that if he allowed himself to think directly about the attack, he would not be able to handle what came up. That conviction shaped the way he related to his own memory. He kept turning away from the event in his mind, and when it intruded anyway it appeared as disconnected visual fragments rather than a narrative he could hold onto. He would tell himself not to go there, not to look too closely, and the result was that the attack remained a set of frightening images he could not put in order even for himself. He felt isolated in this, set apart from coworkers and friends who seemed able to discuss difficult events and move on, while he was left with scenes he could neither fully face nor fully explain.

Arjun’s way of coping became increasingly rigid. He began exercising compulsively, waking before dawn to run hard for miles and spending long evenings pushing through punishing workouts. He described it less as enjoyment than as a way to outrun the agitation in his body and prove to himself that he still had discipline. He also started organizing his life around avoiding anything that might feel stressful. At work he stopped volunteering for public meetings, especially those held near transit hubs, and steered himself toward desk-based tasks with minimal uncertainty. He took circuitous routes across the city to avoid the concourse where the bombing occurred and, more broadly, avoided crowded civic spaces that had once been central to his job. Much of his private time was spent dwelling on who he had been before the attack—more confident, more social, less fragile by his own account.

Over time, these strategies deepened the very conclusions he had drawn about himself. The more Arjun narrowed his world to prevent stress, the more his life seemed to confirm that he was no longer capable. Passing up site visits and high-stakes meetings left him feeling unlike the professional he had trained to be. His excessive exercise became another private standard he could fail against: if he missed a run or felt tired, he took it as evidence of weakness rather than strain. And his constant comparisons with his pre-trauma self hardened his sense that the real Arjun was gone. He became increasingly cut off after his divorce, declining invitations from friends and keeping conversations superficial at the office. In his mind, other people still belonged to ordinary life, while he lived outside it.

By the time he sought help, the loop had tightened. On several recent mornings, after arriving at work and seeing planning maps of the transit district spread across a conference table, he found the same stark images breaking in—the flash, the dust, the red backpack—without sequence, without context, as if the event were happening in separate frames. He would look away, tell himself not to think about it, and feel ashamed that he still could not simply master his own mind. What finally brought him to treatment was a missed presentation on a major station redesign project, work he would once have considered central to his identity. He told the therapist, quietly, that he was frightened not only of the memories but of what they seemed to say about him: that he had become someone smaller, more avoidant, and permanently apart from other people. At the same time, he still hoped there might be a way to face what happened without being overwhelmed by it, and to find some version of himself that did not feel lost.
